¶
'''Bessemer converter, iron, process, steel,''' etc. See the nouns.

'''Bessera''' (bes′e-rä), ''n.'' [NL., named after the Russian naturalist ''Besser''.] A genus of Mexican bulbous liliaceous plants, consisting of a single species, ''B. elegans'', frequently cultivated. Its showy crimson flowers are borne in a terminal umbel.

'''bessis''' (bes′is), ''n.'' Same as ''bes''.

'''bessogne†''', ''n.'' See ''bisogno''.

'''best''' (best), ''a.'' and ''n.'' (superlative of ''good''). [See ''better'', ''a.'', and ''good''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Of the highest quality, excellence, or standing: said of both persons and things in regard to mental, moral, or physical qualities, whether inherent or acquired: as, the ''best'' writers and speakers; the ''best'' families; the ''best'' judgment; the ''best'' years of one’s life; a house built of the ''best'' materials.
{{smaller block|When he is ''best'', he is a little worse than a man; and when he is worst, he is little better than a beast.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 2.}}
<poem>What she wills to do or say
Seems wisest, virtuousest, discreetest, ''best''.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., viii. 550.}}}}

'''2.''' Of greatest advantage, usefulness, or suitability for the purpose intended; most advantageous, suitable, appropriate, or desirable: as, the ''best'' man for the place; the ''best'' way to do anything.
{{smaller block|<poem>His ''best'' companions, innocence and health,
And his ''best'' riches, ignorance of wealth.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 61.}}}}
readings.c2s1:
best-behaved boy in the school; the ''best''-cultivated fields.
{{smaller block|Speak ye, who ''best'' can tell.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 160.}}
<poem>Most solicitous how ''best''
He may compensate for a day of sloth.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv.}}
<poem>He prayeth ''best'' who loveth ''best''
All things both great and small.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', Ancient Mariner, vii. 23.}}}}
'''2.''' In or to the highest degree; to the fullest extent; most fully: as, those who know him ''best'' speak highly of him; those ''best'' informed say so; the ''best''-abused man in town.
{{smaller block|Old fashions please me ''best''. ''Shak.'', T. of the S., iii. 1.

Tell whom thou lovest ''best''. ''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1.

I relish ''best'' the free gifts of Providence.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Old Manse, I.}}}}

'''best''' (best), ''v. t.'' [< ''best'', ''a.'' or ''n.''] '''1.''' To get the better of; outdo; surpass.
{{smaller block|I cannot stand quiet and see the dissenters ''best'' the establishment. ''Trafford'', World in Ch., ii. 77. (''N. E. D.'')}}
'''2.''' To overreach or outwit: as, to ''best'' a client. —'''3.''' To defeat in a contest; do better than; beat; hence, in pugilism, to thrash soundly; drub; defeat at fisticuffs.

'''bestad†.''' An obsolete preterit corresponding to the past participle ''bestead''<sup>3</sup>.

'''bestain''' (bẹ̄-stān′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stain''.] To mark with stains; discolor; spot.
{{smaller block|All with blood ''bestain'' his cheeks.
{{right|''Percy’s Reliques'', p. 134.}}}}

'''bestand''' (bē-stand′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stand''.] To serve; be of service to; be ready to serve or

{{smaller block|To such practical lessons as would always ''bestand'' them well.
{{right|''D. G. Mitchell'', Bound Together.}}}}

¶
'''best-best''' (best′best), ''a.'' The very best: sometimes used in trade to indicate the very best quality.

'''bestead'''<sup>1</sup> (bē-sted′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''besteaded'', ''bested'', ppr. ''besteading''. [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stead'', ''v.'', support, help.] '''1.''' To help; assist.—'''2.''' To profit; benefit; serve; avail.

{{smaller block|Remember this, Gil Blas, . . . pay your court to Signior Rodriguez, . . . his friendship will ''bestead'' you much.
{{right|''Smollett'', tr. of Gil Blas, iii. 3.}}
In this ship was great store of dry Newfoundland fish, . . . the same being so new and good as it did very greatly ''bestead'' us in the whole course of our voyage.
{{right|''Sir F. Drake'', West India Voyage.}}
<poem>Hence, vain deluding Joys,
The brood of Folly without father bred!
How little you ''bested''
Or fill the fixed mind with all your toys!</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Il Penseroso, l. 3.}}}}

'''bestead'''<sup>2</sup>† (bē-sted′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stead'', place.] To take the place of.

{{smaller block|Hys missing of the Vniuersitie Oratorship, wherein Doctor Perne ''besteaded'' him.
{{right|''Nash'', Haue with you to Saffronwalden.}}}}

¶
'''bestead<sup>3</sup>''', ''p. a.'' See ''bested.''

'''bested, bestead''' (bẹ̄-sted′), ''p. a.'' [Prop. only as a pp. or p. a.; but Spenser uses a pret. ''bestad'' and pp. ''bestedded'', and other authors have adopted present forms; < ME. ''bested'', ''bisted'', commonly ''bestad'', ''bistad'', earliest forms ''bistathed'', ''bisteathet'', pp., without pres. or pret. (= Dan. ''bestedt''), < ''be-'' + ''stad'', ''stadd'', later ''sted'', etc., < Icel. ''staddr'' = Sw. ''stadd'', circumstanced, pp. of ''stedhja'', fix, appoint, = AS. ''stæththan'', set, set fast, plant, < ''stæth'', a place, related to ''stede'', a place, stead: see ''stead'' and ''steady''.] '''1.''' Placed; situated: of things.—'''2.''' Placed or circumstanced as to condition, convenience, benefit, and the like; situated: of persons.
{{smaller block|<poem>She saith that she shall not be glad,
Till that she se hym so ''bestad.''</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i.}}
Many far worse ''bestead'' than ourselves. {{right|''Barrow.''}}
<poem>In old Bassora’s schools I seemed
Hermit vowed to books and gloom,—
Ill ''bested'' for gay bridegroom.</poem>
{{right|''Emerson'', Hermione.}}}}
'''3†.''' Disposed mentally; affected: as, “sorrowfully ''bestad,''” ''Chaucer.''—'''4†.''' Provided; furnished.
{{smaller block|The Ladie, ill of friends ''bestedded.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. i. 3.}}}}

'''Bestiæ''' (bes′ti-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., pl. of L. ''bestia'', a beast: see ''beast''.] A suborder of the mammalian order ''Insectivora'', including the true insectivores as distinguished from the frugivorous ''Galeopithecidæ'', having the limbs fitted for walking, but not for flying (being devoid of a parachute), and the lower incisors not pectinate. The group contains the whole of the order, excepting the family just named.

¶
'''bestially''' (bes′tia̤l-i), ''adv.'' In a bestial manner; brutally; as a brute beast.

'''bestian†''' (bes′tian), ''a.'' Of or belonging to the beast spoken of in the Apocalypse (Rev. xiii. xx.).

'''bestianism†''' (bes′tian-izm), ''n.'' [< ''bestian'' + ''-ism.''] The power of the beast. See ''bestian.''

'''bestiarian''' (bes-ti-ā′ri-a̤n), ''n.'' [< L. ''bestia'', a beast, + ''-arian''; suggested by ''humanitarian.''] One who is an advocate of the kind treatment of animals; specifically, in Great Britain, an antivivisectionist.

'''bestiary''' (bes′ti-ā-ri), ''n.'' [< ML. ''bestiarium'', neut. of L. ''bestiarius'', pertaining to wild beasts (as a n., a beast-fighter), < ''bestia'', a wild beast.] '''1†.''' A fighter with wild beasts in the ancient Roman amphitheater.—'''2.''' A name formerly sometimes given to a book treating of animals.
{{smaller block|Mr. Watkins has, however, gone further back, and commences with Homer and Hesiod. His opening chapter, “A Homeric ''Bestiary'',” is one of the most characteristic and satisfactory portions of his work.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 6th ser., XI. 260.}}}}

'''bestiate''' (bes′ti-āt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bestiated'', ppr. ''bestiating.'' [< L. ''bestia'', a beast, + ''-ate''<sup>2</sup>.] To make beastly; bestialize. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Drunkenness ''bestiates'' the heart.
{{right|''R. Junius'', Sinne Stigmatized, p. 235.}}}}

'''bestick''' (bē-stik′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bestuck'', ppr. ''besticking.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stick''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To stick on the surface of; cover over.—'''2.''' To pierce in various places; pierce through and through.
{{smaller block|<poem>Truth shall retire,</poem>}}

{{smaller block|<poem>His ''best'' companions, innocence and health,

{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 61.}}}} '''3.''' Most kind, beneficent, or good: applied to persons: as, the ''best'' husband imaginable; which of your brothers is ''best'' to you?—'''4.''' Largest; greatest; most: as, we spent the ''best'' part of three days in getting there.—{{smaller|'''Best man,''' the groomsman or chief attendant on the bridegroom at a wedding.}}

{{smaller block|I acted in the capacity of backer or ''best man'' to the bridegroom.
{{right|''Dickens.''}}}}

{{smaller block|In our own marriages the ''best man'' seems originally to have been the chief abettor of the bridegroom in the act of capture.
{{right|''Darwin'', Des. of Man, II. xx.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Best work,''' in ''mining'', the richest class of ore.—'''To put one’s best foot foremost.''' See ''foot.''}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' The highest possible state of excellence; the best quality or property of a person or thing.

<poem>Yf thou wylte leve in peas & Reste,
Here, & see, & sey the ''beste.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Prov. of Good Counsel'', 52.}}}}

<poem>But you, O you,
So perfect, and so peerless, are created
Of every creature’s ''best.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 1.}}}}

'''2.''' All that one can do, or show in one’s self: often used in this sense with the possessive pronouns ''my'', ''thy'', ''his'', ''their'', etc.: as, I will do ''my best'' to advance your interests; she is bent on looking ''her best;'' he did all he could to appear at ''his best'' in that performance.

<poem>Then gan I him to comfort all ''my best.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', Daphnaïda, l. 190.}}}}

<poem>Win shall I not, but do ''my best'' to win.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}

{{smaller|'''At best,''' in the utmost degree or extent applicable to the case: as, life is ''at best'' very short.}}

{{smaller block|The Law of England is ''at best'' but the reason of Parliament.{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, x.}}}}

{{smaller|'''For best†''', finally; for good and all.}}
{{smaller block|Those constitutions . . . are now established ''for best'', and not to be mended.{{right|''Milton.''}}}}

{{smaller|'''For the best''', so as to secure the most advantageous result; with the best intentions.—'''The best.''' (''a'') The best people collectively; those of the highest standing in any respect, but especially socially or intellectually.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Throng, their rags and they,
The basest, far into that council-hall
Where sit ''the best'' and stateliest of the land.</poem>{{right|''Tennyson'', Lucretius.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') The best things, or a thing of the best quality: as, he always buys ''the best''; dressed in one’s ''best''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The lads and lassies in their ''best''
Were dressed from top to toe.</poem>{{right|''E. Ransford'', Gypsying.}}}}
{{smaller|'''The best of''', the advantage in (a contest or proceeding or over (a person): as, from the start A. B. had ''the best of'' it.}}
{{smaller block|As far as dignity is concerned, Steele has certainly ''the best of'' the quarrel.
{{right|''A. Dobson'', Introd. to Steele, p. xxxix.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To make the best of''', to use to the best advantage; get all that one can out of.}}
{{smaller block|Let there be freedom to carry their commodities where they may ''make the best of'' them.{{right|''Bacon.''}}}}
{{smaller|Often used in speaking of things or events that are not so good or favorable as was expected or was to be wished: as, ''to make the best of'' ill fortune or a bad bargain.—'''To make the best of one’s way''', to travel or proceed with all possible speed.}}

'''best''' (best), ''adv.'' (superlative of ''well'').   [See ''better'', ''adv.'']   '''1.''' In the most excellent or most suitable manner; with most advantage or success: as, he who runs ''best'' gets the prize; the best-behaved boy in the school; the ''best''-cultivated fields.

{{smaller block|Of shape part human, part ''bestial.''{{right|''Tatler'', No. 49.}}}}
'''2.''' Having the qualities of a beast; brutal; below the dignity of reason or humanity; carnal: as, a ''bestial'' appetite.
{{smaller block|I have lost the immortal part of myself, and what remains is ''bestial.''{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Bestial automaton.''' See ''automaton.''—'''Bestial sign,''' in ''astrol.'', a zodiacal sign denoted by a quadruped, Aries, Taurus, Leo, Sagittarius, or Capricornus.='''Syn.''' ''Brutish'', ''Bestial'', etc. (see ''brute''); vile, depraved, sensual.}}

Stand dumb, and speak not to him.</poem>

{{smaller block|This is the reading of the folios; the quartos and modern editions read ''distilled''.]}}

''bestyrian'', heap up, pile up, < ''be-'' + ''styrian'', stir: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''stir''.]   To put into brisk or vigorous action; reflexively, move with life and vigor: as, ''bestir yourself''.
